Draft content This post is draft content for review. Facts are from the Granite.build README. Granite.build is in alpha, and breaking changes may occur. Fine-tuning a model usually means a pile of scripts: one to download the base model and data, one to train, one to evaluate, and glue to move artifacts between them and between machines. Granite.build replaces the glue with a single pipeline definition.
documents.s: Granite.build: one file from model download to evaluation

documents.t: A Granite.build pipeline lives in a build.yaml file. It declares which models to download, how to fine-tune them, and which evaluations to run, as named targets such as download, fine-tune, and evaluate. Targets are connected through artifact bindings: when a target produces an artifact, the targets that depend on it are dispatched automatically. Artifacts are addressed by URI, so the same pipeline can pull a model from Hugging Face with hf:// and write results to local files, Git, or cloud object storage (file://, git://, cos://).

Each step runs in the environment you choose, without changing the pipeline: Environment Status Docker and local Bash Stable Kubernetes Stable SLURM through SkyPilot Beta RunPod and SkyPilot on AWS Beta The environments, credentials, artifact stores, and step implementations available to a build come from a space, so moving from a laptop to a GPU cluster is a configuration change.

gbserver, the orchestration server, with a REST API and a web dashboard. It watches for pending builds and dispatches them. gb, the command-line client, to submit builds, check status, read logs, and manage artifacts. Lineage tracking, which records where every build, target, and artifact came from. Standalone mode, which uses SQLite and threads, so you can try everything without any external services.

Granite.build ships Agent Skills for coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenCode, so an agent can operate the tool without being taught each time. The gbmcp MCP server lets agents start the backend and run, monitor, and cancel builds. The dashboard also has a chat assistant that only proposes actions: nothing runs until you approve it.
documents.s: Built to work with coding agents

documents.t: You need Python 3.11 or later, plus Node.js 20 or later and yarn for the dashboard. Start the server in standalone mode: git clone https://github.com/ibm-granite/granite.build.git cd granite.build make venv PYTHON=python3.13 source .venv/bin/activate make build-frontend gbserver standalone --space-dir configurations/spaces/local Then, in a second terminal, submit the quickstart build. It runs a single step in a local Bash process, so no Docker is needed: cd granite.build source .venv/bin/activate export GB_ENVIRONMENT=STANDALONE gb build start -f samples/standalone/standalone-quickstart/build.yaml gb build status <build-id> The dashboard is at http://localhost:8080. For everything else, see the Granite.build repository, which is open source under the Apache 2.0 license.

documents.t: Draft content This post is draft content for review. Facts are from the LLMON announcement of November 12, 2026. Every prompt is a mix of things you trust and things you don't. Your system prompt and instructions sit next to retrieved documents, pasted emails, and tool results, and to the model it is all one stream of text. Today we're releasing two experimental Granite models that see that stream differently.
documents.s: LLMON: teaching Granite to tell instructions from data

documents.t: When an instruction is hidden inside a document or a tool result ("ignore the above and…"), a model can follow it as if you had written it. That is indirect prompt injection, and it gets more dangerous as models read more untrusted content on their own, in RAG pipelines and agents. Formats like JSON don't help much. As the announcement puts it, JSON "was designed for parsers, not for causal language models": the brackets and quotes that mark its structure also appear in ordinary text, so the model can't reliably tell where one part ends and the next begins.
documents.s: The problem: everything looks like an instruction

documents.t: LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced "lemon") is a markup language for talking to LLMs. It wraps each part of a prompt, such as an instruction, a document, or a requirement, in a tagged block. The delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so markup can never be confused with content: <|open|>instruction<|close|> Suggest a title for the following email: <|open_end|> <|open|>data<|close|> Dear customer support, I am writing about the wifi on my recent flight... <|open_end|> An exec block then says which instruction runs on which data, much like a function call. Blocks that the exec block doesn't point to are still in context, but the model treats them as input to read, not commands to follow. You rarely write LLMON by hand. The models' chat template renders ordinary chat messages into LLMON, and Mellea converts its LLM calls automatically.

Granite 4.1 3B LLMON preview and Granite 4.1 8B LLMON preview, fine-tuned from the Granite 4.1 base models under the Apache 2.0 license The LLMON toolkit with converters and example notebooks An attention visualization Space that shows how the model's attention follows LLMON blocks

On the OPI prompt injection benchmark, the LLMON models avoided 47% more attacks than the best frontier model and 95% more than the best open-source model. On standard benchmarks, they perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models, so the added robustness doesn't cost general capability. The announcement has the full results.

These are previews, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production. The separation between instructions and data is a learned behavior, not a guarantee, and the benchmarks above cover static, single-turn injections. Attacks that unfold over many turns are still being worked on, so keep your other safeguards, such as Granite Guardian, in place.

Start with the LLMON concept page in these docs for an overview and links. Run a model from its model card, which has a complete prompt example. Read the research: the LLMON language paper and the post-training paper. Tell us what worked, what broke, and which use cases you'd like to see in GitHub Discussions.

Granite is a family of open models from IBM, published under permissive licenses on Hugging Face. This section helps you get oriented, run your first model, understand concepts that apply across all models, and verify what you download. For the latest releases across all families, see What's new.

Each family links to its collection on Hugging Face, where every model card has full details, benchmarks, and usage instructions. Family What it is for Hugging Face Language General purpose instruction-following, text-generation, tool-calling, and agentic capabilities. Collection Switch Modular LLMs that compose a Granite base model, embedded LoRA adapters, and a speech encoder into one checkpoint, so a single endpoint serves chat, decisions, safety checks, and speech-to-text. Collection Vision Understanding images and documents. Collection Speech Speech recognition, bidirectional speech translation, enterprise transcription. Collection Embedding Semantic search, retrieval, and RAG pipelines. Collection Guardian Safety and risk-detection models for identifying harmful content, hallucinations, toxicity, and policy violations in LLM inputs and outputs. Collection Docling Specialist document-parsing model for converting complex PDFs and structured documents into machine-readable formats. Collection Time Series Forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification of enterprise time series data. Collection Libraries Collections of task-specific LoRA adapters (RAG, Guardian, core capabilities) that extend and customize Granite base models without full retraining. Collection

Draft content This page is draft content for review. Granite takes a modular approach to specialized tasks. Instead of training and hosting a separate model for each task, small adapters teach a shared base model one task each. IBM publishes ready-made adapters in Granite Libraries, and Granite Switch composes a base model and its adapters into a single checkpoint that you deploy once. Why this approach: Accuracy on targeted tasks. A small model with the right adapter can match, and sometimes beat, much larger general-purpose models on tasks such as hallucination detection or query rewriting. See the benchmarks in the adapter catalog. One deployment, many capabilities. A single endpoint can serve chat, decisions, safety checks, and RAG steps, using about the same GPU memory as the base model alone. Update parts independently. You can upgrade or swap one adapter without retraining or redeploying the rest, the way you update one dependency in a software project.

A LoRA (low-rank adaptation) adapter is a small set of extra weights trained on top of a base model that stays frozen. Because the base model doesn't change, many adapters can share it, and you can switch between them for different tasks. Standard LoRA has a cost in multi-step workflows. An adapter changes how the model processes the whole conversation, so switching from one adapter to another means processing the conversation again, recomputing the KV cache from scratch. In a RAG workflow that rewrites the query, checks answerability, answers, and then adds citations, that cost repeats at every step. An aLoRA (activated LoRA) adapter only takes effect from an invocation point forward, marked by a control token such as <guardian>. Everything before that point is processed by the base model, so all aLoRA adapters can reuse the same KV cache. The model can move between steps and adapters without reprocessing the conversation, which keeps latency low and throughput high. Granite adapters are also built as adapter functions. Each one is trained for a fixed input and output, such as a score, a choice between options, or a rewritten query, rather than free-form text. A known output format is what lets adapters be called and combined like functions in code. To learn more: Inference-friendly aLoRAs on the IBM Research blog, and the aLoRA paper. How Granite Switch works: control tokens, a shared KV cache, and prefill reuse. The aLoRA vs. LoRA race notebook on Colab, which compares the two on the same model and hardware.

Granite Libraries are collections of ready-made adapters, grouped by purpose: Library Adapters Use it for Core Context attribution, decision, requirement check, uncertainty Explaining which context the model used, picking between fixed options, checking a response against requirements, and calibrated confidence scores RAG Query rewrite, query clarification, context relevance, answerability, hallucination detection, citation generation Each step of an agentic RAG pipeline, before retrieval, before generation, and after generation Guardian Guardian core, factuality detection, factuality correction, policy guardrails Safety risk detection, checking and correcting facts against passages, and policy compliance Things to know: Base models: the r1.0 adapters are trained for Granite 4.0 Micro and the Granite 4.1 3B, 8B, and 30B language models. The decision adapter is available for 4.1 8B and 30B only. An adapter only works with the base model it was trained for. LoRA and aLoRA: every adapter is available as a LoRA, and many also as an aLoRA. Each library's model card lists which. Signed: every adapter is signed. Each library's model card explains how to verify it. See also Verify model signatures. Details per adapter: each adapter has its own README in the library repository, with its inputs, outputs, and evaluation results. You can also compare results in the Granite Libraries evaluation Space. You can use an adapter on its own, loaded on top of its base model, or as part of a Granite Switch model.

A Granite Switch model is a Granite base model with adapters from Granite Libraries embedded in the same checkpoint, and optionally a speech encoder. Each adapter has a control token in the model's chat template, so each request, or each step within a request, selects the adapter it needs. All adapters share the base model's KV cache, so the combined model uses about the same GPU memory as the base model alone. There are two ways to use Switch: Use a pre-composed model. Granite Switch 4.1 8B and 30B combine a Granite 4.1 base model with the decision and Guardian core adapters, plus Granite Speech 5.0 TurboCTC for speech-to-text. One endpoint serves chat, decisions, safety checks, and transcription. The -preview models, in 3B, 8B, and 30B sizes, embed 12 adapters from all three libraries instead. Compose your own. The granite-switch composer combines a base model with the libraries and adapters you choose, and produces a checkpoint that runs in both Transformers and vLLM. The adapter catalog helps you pick adapters and generates the compose command. Because the base model and the adapters are separate parts, Switch models are updated like software. Granite Switch 4.1.1 shipped a new decision adapter and an updated speech model as a backward-compatible patch release. The base model stayed the same. Switch models run with vLLM, using the granite-switch plugin, with Hugging Face Transformers for prototyping, and with llama.cpp using the GGUF variants. To serve decisions through OpenAI's Decisions API format alongside chat, use the granite-switch-decision vLLM plugin.

Preview LLMON and the Granite LLMON models are an experimental preview. They are ready for exploration and evaluation, but not for production use. The language, its special tokens, and the models may change in future releases. Draft content This page is draft content for review. LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced "lemon") is a markup language designed for LLMs. It labels each part of a prompt, such as instructions, data, documents, and tool results, so the model knows exactly what each part is and which parts it should act on.

A typical prompt mixes trusted content, such as your system prompt and instructions, with untrusted content, such as retrieved documents, pasted text, and tool results. To the model, it's all just text. That causes two problems: Prompt injection. An instruction hidden in a document or tool result, such as "ignore the above and…", can be followed as if you wrote it. This is called indirect prompt injection. Confusion about structure. Plain text and JSON don't tell the model reliably where one part ends and the next begins. Smaller models in particular can mix up instructions, data, and requirements. LLMON makes those boundaries explicit. The Granite LLMON models are trained on one rule: only the instructions and system prompt you point the model at are commands. Everything else, including documents, data, and tool results, is input to read, not instructions to follow. In IBM's evaluations, the LLMON models resisted substantially more prompt injection attacks than both frontier and open models, while keeping general capability on par with the Granite 4.1 instruct models. See the announcement for the results. A trained behavior, not a guarantee The separation between instructions and data is learned during training. It reduces the risk of prompt injection, but doesn't eliminate it. The current models address static injections in a single turn. Attacks that unfold over many turns are still being worked on. Keep your other safeguards, such as Granite Guardian, in place.

LLMON wraps each part of a prompt in a tagged block, using reserved special tokens as delimiters so the markup can never be confused with the content. A simplified example: <|open|>instruction<|close|> Suggest a title for the following email: <|open_end|> <|open|>data<|close|> Dear customer support, I am writing about the wifi on my recent flight... <|open_end|> Each block gets an ID, and an exec block then states which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes, much like a function call. Content that the exec block doesn't point to is present but ignored. You don't need to write LLMON by hand: Chat messages: the model's chat template renders ordinary messages into LLMON. You mark which instructions and data the model should act on, and the template does the rest. Mellea: if you build with Mellea, it converts its LLM calls to LLMON automatically. Structured data: the converters in the LLMON repository turn JSON and other structured input into typed, individually addressable blocks. Your own concepts: you can fine-tune an LLMON model with a LoRA adapter to understand domain-specific tags. See Adapters and composition for background, and the fine-tuning examples in the repository.

Model Fine-tuned from Granite 4.1 3B LLMON preview Granite 4.1 3B Base Granite 4.1 8B LLMON preview Granite 4.1 8B Base Both models were released on November 12, 2026, under the Apache 2.0 license, and are part of the Granite Experiments collection. They don't use a conventional chat template, so use the template that ships with the model. Other Granite models aren't trained on LLMON.

A Granite model name is the name of its repository on Hugging Face. Most names follow this pattern, where segments in square brackets appear only when they apply: granite-[family]-<version>-<size>[-<active>][-<variant>][-<format>] Segment Meaning Examples family The model family. Left out for the core language models. speech, vision, guardian, switch version The release the model belongs to. 4.2, 5.0 size Total number of parameters, in billions (b) or millions (m). 3b, 8b, 30b, 470m active For mixture-of-experts models, the number of parameters active for each token. a800m variant A different model within the same family and size. turboctc (faster speech architecture), nc (non-commercial license) format The same weights in another file format or precision. GGUF (llama.cpp, Ollama), fp8, mxfp4, nvfp4 (quantized GPU inference), ONNX, mlx (Apple Silicon, with its own precision such as bf16-mlx or q4-mlx) Some examples: Model name How to read it granite-4.2-8b Language model, version 4.2, 8 billion parameters granite-4.2-8b-GGUF The same model in GGUF format, for llama.cpp and Ollama granite-4.2-3b-q4-mlx Granite 4.2 3B, 4-bit quantized for MLX on Apple Silicon granite-speech-5.0-2b Speech model, version 5.0, 2 billion parameters granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc-nc Speech model, version 5.0, 470 million parameters, TurboCTC architecture, non-commercial license granite-3.1-3b-a800m-instruct Language model from an earlier release, 3 billion parameters with 800 million active per token

Embedding, Time Series, and Granite Libraries models are released on their own schedule. Instead of a version such as 4.2, their names end with a release number: r1, r2, r3, and so on. The rest of the name describes the model, and can include a size, a language, or the model architecture. Model name How to read it granite-embedding-english-r2 English embedding model, release 2 granite-embedding-311m-multilingual-r2 Multilingual embedding model, 311 million parameters, release 2 granite-timeseries-ttm-r3 TinyTimeMixer (TTM) time series model, release 3 granitelib-rag-r1.0 Granite Libraries adapters for RAG, release 1.0 Granite Docling has neither a version nor a release number: granite-docling-258M is the Docling model with 258 million parameters. Other suffixes you may see Older releases and preview models use some additional segments: base: the pretrained model before instruction tuning, as in granite-4.1-8b-base. Models without base are instruction-tuned. instruct: the instruction-tuned model, in releases before 4.0, as in granite-3.1-3b-a800m-instruct. preview: an early release for feedback, which may change before general availability, as in granite-switch-4.1-8b-preview. plus: a variant with additional features, as in granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus, which adds speaker labels and word-level timestamps. nar: a non-autoregressive architecture for higher throughput, as in granite-speech-4.1-2b-nar. h, and sizes named micro, tiny, or small: the hybrid Mamba-transformer architecture and size names used in Granite 4.0, as in granite-4.0-h-tiny. Check the model card for the exact meaning of a suffix.

Each family has its own version numbers. Families are released on their own schedules, so version numbers don't line up across families. For example, the latest speech model is version 5.0 while the latest language models are version 4.2. A higher number in one family doesn't mean it's newer than a model in another family. Versions tell you which models work together. Some models are built on, or designed for, a specific version of another model. Granite Switch 4.1 is built on the Granite 4.1 language models. The Granite Libraries r1.0 adapters are trained for Granite 4.0 Micro and the Granite 4.1 language models, so use them with those base models. The model card lists the base models each model supports. Older releases stay available. These docs and the model selector focus on the latest models, but earlier releases remain on Hugging Face. Each has its own collection, for example Granite 4.1, Granite 4.0, and Granite 3.3. To find out what changed in a release, see What's new.

Draft content This page is draft content for review. Many Granite models are published in several variants: the same model, stored in a different file format or at a different numeric precision. Each variant is its own repository on Hugging Face, named with a format suffix such as -GGUF or -fp8. See Naming and versions. Most variants are quantized: their weights are stored with fewer bits than the original model. A quantized model is a smaller download, needs less memory, and often runs faster, at the cost of some output quality. How much quality you lose depends on the precision, the model size, and your task.

The main repository for a model, for example granite-4.2-8b, holds the full-precision weights in BF16 (bfloat16), stored as safetensors files. BF16 uses 2 bytes per parameter, so Granite 4.2 8B is about 17.6 GB. Use the full-precision model when you: Need the reference quality. The benchmarks on a model card are measured with the full-precision model. Serve on GPUs with enough memory, using Transformers, vLLM, or SGLang. Fine-tune the model, or train adapters for it. The same BF16 precision is also available in other formats: as the bf16 file in the GGUF repository, and as the -bf16-mlx repository for Apple Silicon.

Variant Repository suffix Precision Runs with Hardware GGUF -GGUF Many levels, from 2-bit to 8-bit, plus BF16. One file per level. llama.cpp, Ollama, and other GGUF-based tools CPU, GPU, or both, including laptops FP8 -fp8 8-bit floating point for weights and activations vLLM and other servers that support compressed-tensors checkpoints GPUs with FP8 support, such as NVIDIA Hopper and Ada Lovelace or later MXFP4 -mxfp4 4-bit floating point, in the open microscaling (MX) format vLLM and other servers that support compressed-tensors checkpoints GPUs with FP4 support, such as NVIDIA Blackwell and AMD Instinct MI350 series NVFP4 -nvfp4 4-bit floating point, in NVIDIA's FP4 format vLLM and other servers that support compressed-tensors checkpoints NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs MLX -bf16-mlx, -q8-mlx, -q4-mlx BF16, 8-bit, or 4-bit mlx-lm Apple Silicon Macs (M1 or later) ONNX -ONNX 4-bit weights Transformers.js In the browser, using WebGPU The FP8, MXFP4, and NVFP4 variants are made for GPU serving. They quantize both the weights and the activations, and keep the output layer at full precision. On GPUs without native support for a format, some runtimes fall back to slower kernels or don't load the model at all. Check your runtime's documentation. Not every model has every variant The Granite 4.2 language models are published in all the GPU and MLX formats. Many other models have a GGUF variant only. Embedding, Time Series, and Granite Libraries models, and some speech models, are published at full precision only. To see what's available for a model, open its collection on Hugging Face. Community quantizations On a model's Hugging Face page, Model tree → Quantizations also lists variants made by the community. Only repositories in the ibm-granite organization are published and signed by IBM. See Verify model signatures.

A GGUF repository holds one file per quantization level, for example granite-4.2-8b-Q4_K_M.gguf. The level name tells you how the weights are stored: The number is the approximate bits per weight: Q4 is about 4 bits, Q8 is about 8 bits. K marks the newer k-quant method, which mixes precisions across layers to preserve quality. Q4_0 and Q4_1 are older methods. S, M, and L (small, medium, large) mark how many layers keep a higher precision. Larger means better quality and a bigger file.

Download sizes for the variants of Granite 4.2 8B show how much each precision saves: Precision Variants Download size BF16 (full precision) granite-4.2-8b, -bf16-mlx, GGUF bf16 17.6 GB 8-bit -fp8, GGUF Q8_0, -q8-mlx 9.3–9.6 GB 6-bit GGUF Q6_K 7.2 GB 4-bit -nvfp4, -mxfp4, GGUF Q4_K_M, -q4-mlx 5.0–6.1 GB 2-bit GGUF Q2_K 3.4 GB Running a model takes more memory than its download size, because the context (the KV cache) also needs memory, and it grows with context length. To check which variants fit your hardware, use the model selector.

Start from where the model will run: Laptop or desktop, CPU or mixed CPU and GPU: GGUF with llama.cpp or Ollama. Q4_K_M is a good default, and is the level used in the Quickstart. If you have memory to spare, Q5_K_M, Q6_K, or Q8_0 give output closer to full precision. Use Q3 or Q2 levels only when memory is very limited, because quality drops noticeably. Mac with Apple Silicon: MLX -q4-mlx or -q8-mlx with mlx-lm. GGUF with llama.cpp also runs well on Apple Silicon. Serving on recent NVIDIA GPUs: -fp8 halves memory compared with BF16, with a small quality cost. On Blackwell GPUs, -nvfp4 or -mxfp4 reduce memory further and increase throughput. Evaluating, fine-tuning, or needing reference quality: the full-precision model. In the browser: the ONNX variant, where one is available. Whatever you choose, test the variant on your own prompts before you deploy it. Quantization affects some tasks, such as long reasoning, math, and code, more than others. If quality isn't good enough, try a higher-precision level before you switch to a larger model.

Run Granite 4.2 3B on your own machine with llama.cpp. llama.cpp downloads the model from Hugging Face the first time you run it, and runs on CPU or GPU. This quickstart uses the Q4_K_M quantization from granite-4.2-3b-GGUF. It's a good balance of size and quality for a laptop. For the other quantizations, see Variants and quantization.

macOS and Linux Windows brew install llama.cpp winget install llama.cpp You can also download a prebuilt binary from the llama.cpp releases page, or build it from source. Using the llama app? If you installed llama.cpp through the llama app, it provides a single llama command. Replace the dash with a space and keep the same arguments: llama-cli becomes llama cli, and llama-server becomes llama serve.

llama-cli -hf ibm-granite/granite-4.2-3b-GGUF:Q4_K_M --jinja --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 -hf downloads the model from Hugging Face and caches it locally, so later runs start immediately. --jinja uses the chat template embedded in the model, which Granite needs for chat, tool calling, and thinking. Recent llama.cpp versions turn this on by default; the flag keeps the command working on older versions. --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 are the sampling settings recommended on the model card. Type a prompt at the > prompt. Granite 4.2 reasons step by step inside <think>…</think> before giving its answer. Press Ctrl+C to exit.

To call the model from your own code, start llama-server instead: llama-server -hf ibm-granite/granite-4.2-3b-GGUF:Q4_K_M --jinja --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --port 8080 Then send a request from another terminal: curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What are three uses for a small language model?"}], "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} }' "enable_thinking": false turns off reasoning for a faster, direct answer. Leave it out to keep thinking on. For all thinking modes, see the model card. Not a chat model? Speech, embedding, time series, and Docling models are used through their own libraries rather than a chat runtime. See the model card on Hugging Face for usage.

All Granite models are published on Hugging Face under the ibm-granite organization. To find a model, browse the Granite collections, which group models by family and release. Open the model you're interested in to download its weights and quantized variants, and to read its model card. The model card covers the model's capabilities, benchmarks, license, and detailed usage instructions.

You can run Granite models on your own machine with a local runtime such as: llama.cpp: runs the GGUF variants published on Hugging Face. See the Quickstart above. Ollama: find Granite models in the Ollama library, open the model you want, and follow the instructions on its page.

To serve Granite models on your own infrastructure, use one of the serving frameworks documented on each model card. The model card has the server command, the reasoning and tool-calling parsers to use, and example requests for that model. For example, for Granite 4.2 3B: vLLM: a high-throughput, OpenAI-compatible inference server. See Serving with vLLM. SGLang: an alternative high-throughput serving framework. See Serving with SGLang. To experiment in Python without a server, use Hugging Face Transformers. The model card's example runs the model on an NVIDIA GPU with CUDA. See Quick Start (Transformers). For other models, open the model card from the Granite collections and look for the same sections.

To use Granite without running your own infrastructure, call a hosted model through a cloud provider's API. For example: OpenRouter: access Granite through OpenRouter's OpenAI-compatible API, for example Granite 4.2 8B on OpenRouter. Replicate: run Granite through Replicate's API or web playground, for example Granite 4.2 8B on Replicate. Hugging Face: run models directly from their Hugging Face page through Hugging Face Inference Providers. Open a model in the Granite collections and use the Deploy or Use this model menu on its page. Available providers vary by model. Each provider's model page shows code samples, pricing, and the models it offers.
Concepts: pick the right variant and understand model names. Verify model signatures: confirm your download is authentic.

Draft content This page is draft content for review. Granite models are trained and aligned for safety, but like all language models, they can still produce inaccurate, biased, or unsafe output, and they can be manipulated by adversarial input. Safety in production comes from the whole system: the model, the guardrails around it, and how you test and operate it. Each model card describes the model's known limitations in its Ethical considerations and limitations section.

Granite Guardian models check the prompts going into your application and the responses coming out, and flag risks before they reach users. They run alongside any language model, not only Granite. Granite Guardian 4.1 8B has built-in checks for: Harmful content: general harm, social bias, violence, profanity, sexual content, unethical behavior, and jailbreak attempts. RAG hallucinations: whether retrieved documents are relevant, whether a response is grounded in them, and whether it answers the question. Agentic hallucinations: function calls that don't match the available tools. You can also define your own criteria in plain language, such as a formatting or policy rule. Each check returns a yes or no judgement, with optional reasoning. Choose the option that fits your cost and latency needs: Option Best for Granite Guardian 4.1 8B A separate guardrail model for monitoring, evaluation, and checking inputs and outputs Guardian adapters in Granite Libraries Safety, factuality, and policy checks on the same Granite base model that serves your application, without hosting a second model Granite Guardian HAP 38M Fast, low-cost detection of hate, abuse, and profanity caution Use Guardian models only for the scoring task they're trained for, with the prompt format on the model card. Granite Guardian 4.1 8B is trained and tested on English data only. Test custom criteria before you rely on them. To get started, see the model card and the Granite Guardian cookbooks on GitHub.

In a prompt injection, an attacker hides instructions in content your application passes to the model, such as a retrieved document, a web page, or a tool result. To reduce the risk: Keep untrusted content separate from your instructions. Don't concatenate retrieved or user-supplied text into your system prompt. Check inputs for jailbreak attempts with Granite Guardian before they reach your model. Try LLMON (preview). The Granite LLMON models are trained to follow only the instructions you point them at, and to treat documents and tool results as data. See LLMON. Limit what the model can do. Give agents only the tools and permissions they need, and confirm sensitive actions with a person.

Test your application, not just the model, against the risks that matter for your use case: ARES is IBM's open-source framework for red-teaming AI applications. AI Atlas Nexus and the IBM AI Risk Atlas help you identify and map AI risks for your use case.

Make sure the model you run is the model IBM published: Download Granite models only from the ibm-granite organization on Hugging Face, or from a provider you trust. Variants and fine-tunes published by others aren't reviewed or signed by IBM. Verify the model's signature after you download it, and before you deploy it.

Granite models are developed under IBM's principles for trust and transparency. For IBM's approach to responsible AI, training data transparency, and governance, see Granite trust, safety and security. For the license and training disclosures of each model, see Licensing and disclosures.

To report a security vulnerability or a model safety issue, such as a jailbreak, or harmful or biased output, contact the IBM Product Security Incident Response Team (PSIRT). Include the model name and version, the prompt or steps to reproduce the issue, and the output you received. To learn how IBM handles reported vulnerabilities, see IBM security vulnerability management. IBM also runs an invite-only bug bounty program with HackerOne for security researchers who test Granite models with guardrails in place.

Draft content This page is draft content for review. It replaces the signature verification page on the previous docs site. Experimental Model signing is an experimental feature under active development, and may include breaking changes. IBM signs Granite models using the OpenSSF model signing standard. A signed model's repository on Hugging Face includes a model.sig file, which records a hash of every file in the repository and is signed by IBM. Verifying the signature confirms two things: Integrity: no file has been changed, added, or removed since IBM signed the model. Origin: the model was signed by IBM. Granite models are signed with one of two methods, Sigstore or certificate. The commands are different, so first check which method your model uses.

Install the model-signing tool. It requires Python 3.9 or later. pip install model-signing Download the complete model repository. The signature covers every file, including README.md and images, so a partial download fails verification. For example, with the Hugging Face CLI: hf download ibm-granite/granite-4.2-3b --local-dir granite-4.2-3b cd granite-4.2-3b If you clone with git instead, also run git lfs pull so the model files are downloaded, not just their pointers. Don't add, remove, or edit files in the folder before you verify it.

Check the signature file. If it contains a certificate chain, the model is certificate-signed. Otherwise, it's Sigstore-signed. grep -q x509CertificateChain model.sig && echo "certificate" || echo "sigstore" On Windows PowerShell, use Select-String x509CertificateChain model.sig: any output means certificate-signed. If the repository has no model.sig file, the model isn't signed. Variants are signed separately Each repository is signed on its own. A quantized variant, such as -GGUF or -fp8, can use a different method from its main model, or not be signed at all. Always check the model.sig in the repository you downloaded. Run this command in the model folder: model_signing verify sigstore \ --signature model.sig \ --ignore-paths .cache \ --identity Granite-sign@ibm.com \ --identity_provider https://sigstore.verify.ibm.com/oauth2 \ . --identity and --identity_provider check that the model was signed by IBM's Granite signing identity. --ignore-paths .cache skips the cache folder that the Hugging Face CLI creates. You can leave it in for other download methods. A successful verification ends with: Verification succeeded Before that line, you might also see Key ... failed to verify root. This message comes from Sigstore updating its trust data, and isn't an error.

Download the DigiCert root certificate: curl https://cacerts.digicert.com/DigiCertTrustedRootG4.crt.pem -o DigiCertTrustedRootG4.crt.pem Run this command in the model folder, using the path where you saved the certificate: model_signing verify certificate \ --signature model.sig \ --ignore-paths .cache \ --log_fingerprints \ --certificate_chain /path/to/DigiCertTrustedRootG4.crt.pem \ . Here, --ignore-paths .cache is required if you downloaded with the Hugging Face CLI. The signatures for some certificate-signed models don't exclude the CLI's cache folder. Check the output. A successful verification shows these three certificate fingerprints, followed by Verification succeeded: [ init ] sha256 Fingerprint: 55:2F:7B:DC:F1:A7:AF:9E:6C:E6:72:01:7F:4F:12:AB:F7:72:40:C7:8E:76:1A:C2:03:D1:D9:D2:0A:C8:99:88 [ verify ] sha256 Fingerprint: 46:01:1E:DE:1C:14:7E:B2:BC:73:1A:53:9B:7C:04:7B:7E:E9:3E:48:B9:D3:C3:BA:71:0C:E1:32:BB:DF:AC:6B [ verify ] sha256 Fingerprint: F2:9F:3F:0F:7E:95:41:60:14:69:D8:E6:44:9C:93:54:43:A0:BA:91:89:57:EE:49:CA:FC:64:AD:6E:1D:96:02 Verification succeeded The fingerprints identify, in order, the DigiCert root certificate, DigiCert's code signing certificate, and IBM's signing certificate. If any fingerprint is different, don't use the model. note IBM's current signing certificate expires on November 1, 2027. Models signed after it's renewed will show a different last fingerprint, and this page will be updated.

Granite Libraries repositories are signed per adapter rather than as a whole. Each adapter folder, for example decision/granite-4.1-8b/lora/, has its own model.sig that covers the files in that folder. Download the adapter you want: hf download ibm-granite/granitelib-core-r1.0 \ --include "decision/granite-4.1-8b/lora/*" \ --local-dir granitelib-core-r1.0 cd granitelib-core-r1.0/decision/granite-4.1-8b/lora Find the signing method in that folder, and verify it with the matching command. Most adapters are Sigstore-signed. The decision adapters are certificate-signed.

Error What it means What to do Extra files found in model The folder has files that weren't signed. If the file is in .cache, add --ignore-paths .cache. Otherwise, remove the files you added, or download the model again into an empty folder. Missing files in model The download is incomplete. Download the complete repository, not only the model weights. Hash mismatch for '<file>' A file is different from the one IBM signed. Download the model again. If you cloned with git, run git lfs pull. If it still fails, don't use the model. Certificate's SANs do not match The signer identity in your command is wrong. Use --identity Granite-sign@ibm.com. Earlier instructions used a different identity. To learn more about the tool and its options, see the model-signing documentation.

November 12, 2026 · Language (preview) LLMON is a new markup language that labels each part of a prompt, so the model can tell your instructions apart from the documents, data, and tool results it should only read. The Granite 4.1 3B and 8B LLMON preview models are trained to follow only the instructions they're pointed at, which makes them more resistant to prompt injection. These are experimental models, for exploration and evaluation rather than production use. See LLMON. Granite 4.1 3B LLMON preview · Granite 4.1 8B LLMON preview · Announcement

October 27, 2026 · Switch Granite Switch 4.1.1 updates the 8B and 30B Switch models with new weights for the decision adapter. Like the 4.1 release, a single endpoint serves chat, decisions, safety checks, and speech-to-text. This release shows how Switch models can be updated one adapter at a time, without replacing the whole model. Granite Switch 4.1 8B · Granite Switch 4.1 30B · Announcement

October 21, 2026 · Speech Granite Speech 5.0 470M TurboCTC, built for high-throughput batch transcription, now supports seven languages: English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, and Japanese. It also adds native punctuation and capitalization, and improves English accuracy. A variant under a non-commercial license is also available. Granite Speech 5.0 470M TurboCTC · Non-commercial variant

October 20, 2026 · Speech Granite Speech 5.0 2B is a compact speech-language model for multilingual speech recognition and bidirectional speech translation in English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese. Compared to Granite Speech 4.1 2B, it has the same parameter count, with higher English transcription accuracy and better robustness to noise, reverberation, and distant microphones. Granite Speech 5.0 2B · Granite Speech collection

October 14, 2026 · Switch Granite Switch is a new family of modular models. Each Switch model combines a Granite 4.1 language model, task-specific adapters, and a speech encoder in one checkpoint, so a single endpoint can serve chat, decisions, safety checks, and speech-to-text. Adapters are selected per request. See Adapters and composition. Granite Switch collection

August 25, 2026 · Language Granite 4.2 adds built-in reasoning to the language models, in 3B, 8B, and 30B sizes. The models reason step by step inside <think>…</think> before answering, which improves math, coding, multi-step logic, and tool calling. You can switch between full thinking, non-thinking, and low-effort modes for each request. Each model is also published in GGUF, fp8, mxfp4, nvfp4, and MLX formats.
